## China’s Rise to Manufacturing Dominance (2000-2030P)

This was originally posted on our Voronoi app. Download the app for free on iOS or Android and discover incredible data-driven charts from a variety of trusted sources.

China and manufacturing dominance together are words easily believed, but this wasn’t always the case. The world’s manufacturer didn’t always make—quite literally—everything. 

This visualization projects the change in manufacturing value added (MVA) by country from 2000 to 2030.

Data is sourced from the UN Industrial Development Organization, as of November 2024.

## Economic Reforms and Exports Drove China’s Boom

Back in 2000, China accounted for only 6% of global manufacturing value added (MVA), easily eclipsed by manufacturing giants like the U.S., Japan, and Germany, not to mention a host of other high income countries.

All of that changed when China joined the WTO in 2001, giving it better trade deals with other members. At the same time the government significantly opened up the economy, allowing foreign direct investment into several key sectors, prompting a take off in new business growth.

| Countries | Share of MVA (2000) | Countries | Share of MVA (2030P) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 🇺🇸 U.S. | 25% | 🇨🇳 China | 45% (+39pp) |
| 🇯🇵 Japan | 11% | 🇺🇸 U.S. | 11% (-14pp) |
| 🇩🇪 Germany | 8% | 🇯🇵 Japan | 5% (-6pp) |
| 🇨🇳 China | 6% | 🇩🇪 Germany | 3% (-5pp) |
| 🇮🇹 Italy | 4% | 🇰🇷 South Korea | 3% |
| 🇫🇷 France | 3% | Other High Income Countries | 16% |
| 🇬🇧 UK | 3% | Upper Middle Income Countries | 8% |
| Other High Income Countries | 21% | Low & Lower Middle Income Countries | 9% |
| Upper Middle Income Countries | 14% | N/A | N/A |
| Low & Lower Middle Income Countries | 5% | N/A | N/A |

Previous decades of economic reforms—transforming the country from an agrarian society to an industrial one—and mix of free-market socialism had primed the country to emerge as a global manufacturer.

A vast skilled workforce, which is far more affordable than those in high income countries, helped supercharge growth. At one point in the mid-2000s, exports accounted for a full-third of China’s GDP.

And these exports covered everything: electronics, machinery, consumer goods, textiles, even something as specific as shipbuilding. 

By 2030, the UN projects that China will account for 45% of global manufacturing value added (MVA), far away the highest share held by a single country. The U.S., at 11% is expected to be a distant second.

## Which Boys’ Names Are Most Popular Across the U.S.?

### Key Takeaways

- Liam has been America’s top boy’s name for nine straight years, but it led only 15 states in 2025, down from 23 a year earlier.
- Noah (14 states), Oliver (12), and Theodore (6) led most of the remaining states. Theodore topped just one state in 2024.
- West Virginia’s favorite was Waylon, a name that had never topped any state before.

The most popular boys’ names vary widely across the U.S., with some dominating entire regions and others claiming the top spot in just one state.

This map shows the most popular name given to baby boys born in 2025 in every U.S. state and D.C., using data from the Social Security Administration. The agency counts names from Social Security card applications, organized by state of birth.

## Liam Leads 15 States, Including the Three Largest

Just four names topped the rankings in 47 states. Liam, Noah, and Oliver remained the dominant favorites, but Theodore emerged as a serious contender, leading six states after topping just one in 2024.

Each name has its own territory. Liam led much of the Sun Belt, including California, Texas, and Florida, while Noah topped many East Coast states, from Massachusetts to South Carolina. Oliver’s states stretch across the Midwest and Mountain West, while Theodore’s are mostly northern: Maine, New Hampshire, Michigan, and Minnesota, along with Kansas and Wyoming.

The three largest states help explain how Liam remains No. 1 nationally while leading relatively few states. About 7,200 of the country’s 20,800 Liams were born in California, Texas, or Florida, and the name finished second in 17 other states. As with America’s favorite dog breeds by state, the national ranking gives more weight to populous states.

These close races reflect how much baby-name preferences have diversified. Liam was given to about 1.1% of boys born in 2025, or one in every 88, according to the agency’s national data. In 1950, the top name, James, accounted for 4.7% of boys. With parents choosing from a wider variety of names, just 27 Theodores were enough to lead Wyoming.

## Noah and Theodore Are Gaining on Liam

The map looked different a year earlier. Liam led 23 states in 2024, compared with just six for Noah. In 2025, seven states switched directly from Liam to Noah, including New York, where Liam had held the top spot for 10 straight years. Nationally, Liam’s lead over Noah shrank from about 1,800 babies to just 460.

## Which Cities Are the Most and Least Stressful?

### Key Takeaways

- New York ranks as the world’s most stressed city, with Dublin close behind.
- A 10 km journey in Dublin takes more than twice as long as in cities on the “least stressed” list.
- Four Dutch cities rank among the world’s 10 least stressed.

Major cities offer access to jobs and opportunities, but often at the cost of longer commutes, higher expenses, and everyday pressures.

Yet the most stressful cities aren’t necessarily the largest, with some smaller European cities ranking surprisingly high.

This visualization uses data from Remitly, which analyzed 170 cities using information collected in October 2025. Each city received a stress score out of 10 based on travel times, cost of living, healthcare quality, perceived crime, and air pollution.

The scores reflect urban living conditions rather than residents’ self-reported stress.

## The World’s 10 Most Stressed Cities

New York’s fast-paced reputation makes its top ranking unsurprising. Dublin, however, finishes almost level with it, ahead of much larger cities such as Mexico City, Manila, and London.

Traffic helps explain Dublin’s position, with congestion making travel unusually slow for a city of its size.

The table below ranks the 10 cities with the highest stress scores.

| Rank | City | Country | Stress Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | New York | USA | 7.56 |
| 2 | Dublin | Ireland | 7.55 |
| 3 | Mexico City | Mexico | 7.38 |
| 4 | Manila | Philippines | 7.34 |
| 5 | London | UK | 7.25 |
| 6 | Milan | Italy | 7.25 |
| 7 | Athens | Greece | 7.23 |
| 8 | São Paulo | Brazil | 7.14 |
| 9 | Turin | Italy | 6.90 |
| 10 | Kolkata | India | 6.89 |

New York ranks first with a score of 7.56, just 0.01 points ahead of Dublin. While New York has particularly high living costs, Dublin stands out for its traffic.

According to Remitly, driving 10 km in Dublin takes around 32 minutes, compared with an average of 21 minutes across the cities studied. That’s roughly 50% longer than the sample average.

Kolkata, which ranks 10th overall, has the slowest travel times in the dataset. A 10 km journey takes an average of 34 minutes and 33 seconds, more than three times as long as in San Antonio, Texas, the fastest city at 10 minutes and 13 seconds.

Europe also features prominently, with Dublin, London, Milan, Turin, and Athens all appearing among the 10 most stressed cities.

## The World’s 10 Least Stressed Cities

At the opposite end of the ranking, the Netherlands stands out. Eindhoven and Utrecht occupy the top two spots, with two other Dutch cities also making the top 10.

The contrast with Dublin is striking, as cities in these two relatively wealthy European countries perform very differently on Remitly’s measures of urban stress.

The table below shows the 10 cities with the lowest stress scores.

| Rank | City | Country | Stress Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Eindhoven | Netherlands | 2.34 |
| 2 | Utrecht | Netherlands | 2.67 |
| 3 | Canberra | Australia | 2.80 |
| 4 | Tallinn | Estonia | 2.83 |
| 5 | Gronigen | Netherlands | 2.84 |
| 6 | Trondheim | Norway | 2.84 |
| 7 | Bergen | Norway | 2.85 |
| 8 | Porto | Portugal | 2.97 |
| 9 | Brisbane | Australia | 2.98 |
| 10 | Rotterdam | Netherlands | 3.34 |

Eindhoven ranks as the world’s least stressed city, scoring just 2.34 thanks in part to shorter commutes, strong healthcare scores, and low perceived crime.

A 10 km journey takes just under 15 minutes in Eindhoven, compared with approximately 32 minutes in Dublin.
